topics.title: Digital foundations
summary: Four technological layers: Energy (foundation) → Hardware (physical) → Telecommunications (connectivity) → Software (abstract).
Without telecommunications computing is local; connectivity makes it global and collaborative.
Connectivity evolution: Internet (computers) → Mobile (people) → Cloud (resources) → APIs (services) → Platforms (markets & ecosystems).
Connectivity creates value AND vulnerability → cybersecurity + privacy + digital trust become central.
3D printing = additive manufacturing = Digital → Physical. Digital twin = Physical → Digital (monitor, simulate, predict before acting).
AR = augment reality (overlay); VR = replace reality; MR = integrate and interact with digital objects in physical space.
The value of immersive tech is not the virtual world but what it lets firms do in the real world (design, manufacturing, training, CX, remote collaboration).
Digital platform = technology-enabled business model facilitating exchanges between user groups; shift from connecting technology to orchestrating interactions.
Digital (binary 0/1) vs analog (continuous pulses): digital is cheaper, encryptable, mergeable, error-correcting.
cards: Four technological layers of the digital economy
Internet (connected computers) → Mobile (people) → Cloud (resources) → APIs (services) → Platforms (markets/ecosystems)
3D printing: digital → physical (additive, layer by layer). Digital twin: physical → digital (monitor, simulate, predict).
AR overlays digital info on reality; VR replaces reality; MR integrates interactive digital objects into physical space.
Large, powerful centralized computer for high-volume, mission-critical transactions with many concurrent users (e.g. banks).
Connectivity creates value but also vulnerability → cybersecurity, privacy, digital trust.
Subtractive removes material from a block; additive builds layer by layer from a digital design (less waste, complex shapes, customization).
Early computer: ~180,000 thermionic valves, ~180 m² — shows how huge early computing infrastructure was.

mcq.q: Which ordering correctly describes the four technological layers of the digital economy, from foundation upward?
mcq.e: Energy powers everything; hardware is the physical layer; telecom connects; software is the abstract layer that tells hardware what to do.

mcq.q: In the connectivity evolution, what did APIs connect?
mcq.e: Internet connected computers, mobile connected people, cloud connected resources, APIs connected services, platforms connected markets.

mcq.q: A company builds a virtual replica of its production line, fed by sensor data, to test a layout change before touching the real plant. This is:
mcq.e: A digital twin is a digital representation of a physical asset used to monitor, simulate and predict before acting (physical → digital).

mcq.q: Which statement best distinguishes MR from AR?
o: In MR digital objects are integrated into physical space and can be interacted with; in AR information is overlaid on reality
In MR the physical world is fully replaced by a digital one
AR requires a headset while MR works only on smartphones
AR is used for training while MR is used for design
mcq.e: AR = augment (overlay). VR = replace. MR = integrate and interact.

mcq.q: Which digital development is associated with the new exposure 'expanded attack surface'?
mcq.e: Internet → network attacks; mobile → identity/device risk; cloud → distributed infrastructure; data & IoT → privacy; APIs & platforms → expanded attack surface.

mcq.q: According to the lecture, where does the business value of immersive technologies lie?
o: In what the virtual layer allows companies to do in the real world
In the quality of the virtual environment itself
In reducing energy consumption of data centres
mcq.e: Core principle: the value is not the virtual world but its real-world uses — design, manufacturing, training, CX, remote collaboration.

mcq.q: Which is NOT listed as a benefit of 3D printing?
o: Higher economies of scale for standardized mass products
mcq.e: 3D printing enables design freedom, faster time to market, customization, less waste and complex shapes — it is not about mass standardization.

mcq.q: The strategic shift represented by a digital platform is from:
mcq.e: A platform is not merely technology; it becomes an architecture for exchange that orchestrates interactions.

tf: 3D printing converts physical objects into digital information.
That is the digital twin direction. 3D printing goes digital → physical.
Without telecommunications, computing remains local.
Connectivity makes computing global and collaborative.
VR overlays digital information onto the real world.
That is AR. VR replaces the physical environment with a fully simulated one.

topics.title: Industrial revolutions
summary: Industrial revolution = technological change + production transformation + organizational transformation.
1.0 (~1760–1840, Britain): steam & water → MECHANIZATION, factory system.
2.0 (~1870–1914): electricity, assembly line → MASS PRODUCTION (standardization, division of labour, specialization, economies of scale).

Ford = standardization + limited variety + scale + centralization. Sloan (GM) = differentiation (Chevrolet, Buick, Cadillac) + decentralization (semi-autonomous divisions, HQ controls strategy/finance).
3.0 (from ~1970s): electronics, computers, PLCs, robots → AUTOMATION. Limitation: systems not interconnected.
4.0 (from ~2011, Hannover Fair): IoT, AI, CPS, big data, cloud, digital twins → CONNECTED + INTELLIGENT production. An automated machine is not automatically Industry 4.0.
IoT = connect (objects + data exchange). CPS = connect + compute + control (digital system acts on the physical process).
Mechanization = machine reduces physical effort, human operates. Automation = system operates with reduced human intervention.
Push = forecast → produce → inventory → sell (overproduction risk). Pull = demand → produce → deliver (delay/capacity risk).
VUCA = Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, Ambiguity → need for flexibility and adaptability.
Red ocean = compete in existing market for existing demand. Blue ocean = create new market space.
Industry 5.0 (emerging concept, not a 5th historical revolution) = human-centric + sustainable + resilient; builds on 4.0.
Human role: operates → specializes → programs/supervises → works with digital systems → collaborates with technology.

mcq.q: A company splits into semi-autonomous divisions managing their own products, while headquarters controls strategy, finance and performance. This reflects:
mcq.e: Sloan at GM: decentralized operations + coordinated central control. The notes flag this as a likely MCQ.

mcq.q: What distinguishes Industry 4.0 from Industry 3.0?
o: Machines and systems are connected, exchange data and coordinate decisions
Steam replaces human and animal power
mcq.e: 3.0 = automation, systems may operate separately. 4.0 = connected + intelligent automation with data-driven optimization.

mcq.q: Which is the key difference between IoT and a cyber-physical system?
o: A CPS also computes and controls the physical process, not just connects and exchanges data
IoT controls machines while CPS only collects data
CPS is a 3.0 technology while IoT is 4.0
IoT uses software while CPS uses only hardware
mcq.e: IoT = connect. CPS = connect + compute + control.

mcq.q: A clothing brand forecasts winter demand and produces 100,000 jackets before knowing actual sales. Its main risk is:
mcq.e: That's a push strategy; the main risk is overproduction. Pull's main risk is delays.

mcq.q: Which event does the lecture associate with the emergence of Industry 4.0?
mcq.e: Industry 4.0 is associated with the 2011 Hannover Fair in Germany.

mcq.q: Which statement about Industry 5.0 is correct?
o: It is an emerging concept that builds on 4.0 technologies, adding human-centricity, sustainability and resilience
It is the universally recognized fifth historical industrial revolution
It replaces Industry 4.0 technologies with human labour
It is defined by the introduction of electricity
mcq.e: Industry 5.0 is an extension/emerging concept, not one of the four historical revolutions.

mcq.q: A worker operating a powered mechanical loom is an example of:
mcq.e: Mechanization: machines reduce physical effort but humans still directly operate them. A programmed robot doing it alone = automation.

mcq.q: In VUCA, 'ambiguity' refers to:
o: Situations with multiple interpretations and unclear cause-and-effect
mcq.e: Volatility = rapid change; uncertainty = hard to predict; complexity = many interconnected variables; ambiguity = multiple interpretations.

mcq.q: Ford's organizational logic is best summarized as:
mcq.e: Ford = standardization, mass production, economies of scale, centralization.

mcq.q: What role do humans play in Industry 3.0 according to the evolution of the human role?
mcq.e: 1.0 operates; 2.0 specializes; 3.0 programs/supervises; 4.0 works with connected systems; 5.0 collaborates.

mcq.q: A company creates a new market space where direct competition is initially irrelevant. This is a:
mcq.e: Blue ocean = create new market space / new demand.

mcq.q: Which limitation of Industry 3.0 is crucial for understanding Industry 4.0?
o: Automated systems were not necessarily interconnected or continuously exchanging information
Machines could not perform tasks without humans operating them
Electricity was not yet available in factories
mcq.e: 4.0 adds connectivity, information exchange and intelligence to automation.

tf: An automated machine is automatically an Industry 4.0 system.
Key exam rule: 4.0 requires connectivity, data exchange and intelligence, not just automation.
Pull production is triggered by actual customer demand.
Demand → produce → deliver.
Sloan's approach emphasized one standardized product for all customers.
That is Ford. Sloan used differentiation: different brands for different segments.
Industry 1.0 started in Great Britain around 1760.
Approximately 1760–1840, beginning in Great Britain.

topics.title: Guest lecture: Google & Google Cloud

Alphabet = core Google + AI + Cloud + Other Bets + investments (Waymo, Nest, Google X, DeepMind, GV, Anthropic investment) → portfolio diversification.
Google X moonshot = aim for 10× better, not 10% better.
Five principles of innovation: Focus on the user; Fail quickly and learn; Share everything; Data, not opinions; Let people pursue their dreams.
Four strategic pillars: vertical integration in AI; monetization shift (beyond CPC ads to subscriptions); capital infrastructure expansion (data centres); portfolio diversification.
GCP lecture figures: ~1 billion users, 43 regions; Italian regions Milan + Turin.
AI figures: $4.4T opportunity; 40% of enterprise apps with agents by end 2026; 52% already deployed agents.
Chatbot = conversation (user asks, AI answers). Agent = goal + tools + actions (plan, act, evaluate, iterate).
Search engine → answer engine (direct synthesized answers) → implications for SEO, ads, Google's model.
Open source logic: the more you share, the more you receive from the ecosystem.
Culture: 10× thinking, data-driven decisions, OKRs (Objective = what; Key Results = how measured), pivot to AI speed.
Traditional IT = store + compute. AI-native = connect data + analyze + predict + automate + act.
cards: Focus on the user; fail quickly and learn; share everything; data not opinions; let people pursue their dreams
Vertical integration in AI; monetization shift; capital infrastructure expansion; portfolio diversification

mcq.q: Google controlling infrastructure, chips, cloud, models and applications for AI illustrates:

mcq.q: What distinguishes an AI agent from a chatbot?
o: It pursues a goal, uses tools and performs actions
It answers questions in natural language
It has no access to external systems

mcq.q: Which two Italian cities host Google Cloud regions according to the lecture?
mcq.e: Milan + Turin, due to concentration of tech companies, banks and enterprise customers.

mcq.q: According to the lecture, Google's open-source strategy rests on the idea that:
o: The more you share, the more you can receive from the ecosystem
Technology should be protected to maintain monopoly rents
Open source reduces the need for data centres

mcq.q: Which statement about Google's 'monetization shift' is correct?
o: AI may require revenue models beyond search advertising such as subscriptions and paid AI services
Google is abandoning cloud for advertising
Cost-per-click is becoming Google's only revenue model
Google plans to monetize by selling user data directly

mcq.q: Google investing in Anthropic illustrates that innovation can come from:
o: Outside the organization as well as inside

Cloud is not abstract: data centres, servers, storage, fibre networks.

topics.title: Five domains & digital competition
summary: Digital transformation is a matter of strategy and mindset, not just technology.
Five domains of strategy that digital is changing (Rogers): Customers, Competition, Data, Innovation, Value.

Customers: mass market → dynamic customer networks. Competition: defined industries → fluid boundaries, platforms, co-opetition. Data: expensive operational resource → strategic intangible asset. Innovation: internal, finished products → experimentation, internal + external. Value: defined by industry → defined by evolving customer needs.
Digital unbundles activities: fragmentation (value chain broken up, e.g. Amazon logistics), new entrants (Apple/Google in payments), convergence (Apple Watch in health).
Competitors may no longer come from your own industry — boundaries are blurring.
Asset-light giants: Uber owns no vehicles; Facebook creates no content; Alibaba holds no inventory; Airbnb owns no real estate.
Ecosystem = network satisfying customer needs by connecting value chains; competition increasingly between ecosystems (e.g. Tesla car as smart home; Uber delivering vaccines).
TikTok: from app to platform (1bn users) → social commerce.
cards: The traditional value chain is broken into separate activities that new players can enter (e.g. Amazon in logistics).
Companies enter adjacent industries, blurring boundaries (e.g. Apple Watch/Fitbit in health monitoring).
Analog: expensive operational resource. Digital: strategic intangible asset generated continuously.
Analog: mass market audience. Digital: dynamic customer networks.

mcq.q: Which list correctly names the five domains of digital transformation?
mcq.e: Rogers' five domains: Customers, Competition, Data, Innovation, Value.

mcq.q: Apple and Google entering the payments business is an example of:
mcq.e: The lecture uses Apple/Google payments as the 'new entrants' example.

mcq.q: Apple Watch and Fitbit offering health monitoring illustrate:
mcq.e: Convergence: companies enter adjacent industries.

mcq.q: 'Uber — the largest transportation company that owns no vehicles' illustrates the shift from:
o: Owning assets to orchestrating participants who create value
mcq.e: Digital firms orchestrate value rather than owning everything.

mcq.q: In the digital economy, how is value defined according to the five-domain recap?
mcq.e: Analog: value defined by industry. Digital: defined by changing customer needs.

tf: In the digital economy, a firm's main competitor always comes from its own industry.
Boundaries blur; competitors can come from outside the industry.
Digital transformation is primarily a matter of technology rather than strategy.
The course repeatedly stresses: strategy and mindset, not merely technology.

topics.title: Platforms & sharing economy
summary: Platform = business creating value by facilitating direct interactions between two or more distinct types of customers. Properties: distinct groups, direct interaction, facilitation.
Pipeline/linear: company → product → customer (value FOR customers). Platform: producer ↔ platform ↔ consumer (value BY connecting participants).
Four platform types: exchange (eBay, Airbnb, Uber); transaction system (payments); ad-supported media; hardware/software standard (OS, consoles).
Network effects: direct/same-side (more WhatsApp users) and cross-side/indirect (more buyers ↔ more sellers).
Why platforms scale: frictionless acquisition (web, APIs, SDKs), scalable growth (cloud), on-demand access (mobile), trust (authentication, reputation).
Platform strategy questions: participants, value, network effects, governance. Revenue: transaction fees, membership, advertising, direct sales, services.
Product → service → platform → ecosystem: products create value, platforms enable value, ecosystems multiply value.
Co-opetition = cooperate to grow the pie, compete to divide it.
Symmetric competitors = similar VP + similar business model (BMW vs Mercedes). Asymmetric = similar need + different business model (BMW vs Uber).
Disintermediation = remove middleman (travel agency). Intermediation = new platform inserts itself (publisher → Facebook → reader).
Competitive value train: originator → producer → distributor → consumer; analyze value exchange, symmetric & asymmetric competitors; gain leverage.
Power to the unique value creator (IP, brand, network effects) and power to the ends. Smiling curve: high value at R&D and brand/services, low in manufacturing.
Sharing economy: ownership → access; P2P. Four principles of collaborative consumption: critical mass, idling capacity, belief in the commons, trust between strangers.
Sharing economy enabled by platform + smartphone + digital access + payments & geolocation. Risks: regulation/tax, worker protection, safety/privacy, externalities, platform power.
B2B sharing motivations: economic, social, ecological (circular economy).
Google ecosystem = data + AI + digital services. Amazon = commerce + logistics + cloud (AWS) + network effects.

Distinct customer groups, direct interaction, facilitation

Direct: more users on the same side add value (WhatsApp). Cross-side: more on one side add value for the other (buyers ↔ sellers).

Participants, value exchanged, network effects, governance
Competition + cooperation: cooperate to grow the pie, compete to divide it.
Symmetric: similar VP + similar model (BMW vs Mercedes). Asymmetric: similar need + different model (BMW vs Uber).
Remove a middleman vs a new intermediary/platform inserts itself between firm and customer.
Value high at R&D/technology and brand/marketing/services ends, low in manufacturing.
Critical mass, idling capacity, belief in the commons, trust between strangers
Originator → producer → distributor → consumer; analyze value exchange and symmetric/asymmetric competitors to gain leverage.
API: way for software to communicate with other software. SDK: developer toolkit to build with a technology.

mcq.q: Why is Skype (person-to-person calls) NOT a platform under the course definition?
o: Its customers are all of the same type, not distinct groups
It does not use the internet
It has no network effects at all
mcq.e: Platforms require two or more distinct types of customers (e.g. buyers and sellers).

mcq.q: Mobile operating systems and game consoles belong to which platform type?
mcq.e: They provide a standard used by other participants (developers).

mcq.q: More drivers on Uber improve availability for riders, which attracts more riders. This is a:
mcq.e: Value increases for the other side of the platform.

mcq.q: BMW and Uber are best described as:
o: Members of the same value train stage
mcq.e: Similar customer need (mobility), different business models.

mcq.q: A publisher must now reach readers through Facebook's feed, which captures part of the value. This is:
mcq.e: A new platform intermediary inserts itself between the company and customer.

mcq.q: According to the smiling curve, which activity typically captures the LEAST value?
mcq.e: Value is higher at both ends, lower in the middle (fabrication).

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the four principles of collaborative consumption?
mcq.e: The four: critical mass, idling capacity, belief in the commons, trust between strangers.

mcq.q: Which platform-scaling driver is linked to authentication, verification and reputation systems?
mcq.e: Trust increases confidence between participants who don't know each other.

mcq.q: 'Products create value, platforms ___ value, ecosystems ___ value.'
mcq.e: Product → service → platform (enable) → ecosystem (multiply, via orchestration).

mcq.q: Which question belongs to the 'governance' dimension of platform strategy?
o: Who controls access, standards, ranking, fees, data and trust?
Why does value grow with size?
mcq.e: Participants / value / network effects / governance.

mcq.q: Amazon Prime is an example of which platform revenue model?
mcq.e: Subscriptions = membership fees.

mcq.q: In the competitive value train, 'power to the ends' means:
o: The first creator and the final customer interface have the most leverage; middle players are easier to bypass
The last company to enter the market wins
Power always belongs to the distributor
Consumers hold no power in digital markets
mcq.e: Ends = originator and customer interface; links to the smiling curve.

mcq.q: B2B sharing motivated by reusing resources and reducing new production connects to which motivation?
mcq.e: Economic = utilization/profit; social = share skills; ecological = circular economy.

tf: In a pipeline business, value is created mainly by connecting participants.
Pipeline creates value FOR customers; platform creates value BY connecting participants.
Network effects can contribute to highly concentrated markets.
Self-reinforcing growth loops can create winner-takes-all dynamics.
Access-based consumption means customers get the benefits of an asset without necessarily owning it.
e.g. car sharing, coworking, SaaS.

topics.title: New consumer profile & omnichannel
summary: New consumer: hyper-informed, less loyal, omnichannel, networked.
Digital customer journey (awareness → consideration → purchase → experience → loyalty) is non-linear; manage the whole experience.
Multichannel = several channels. Omnichannel = channels integrated into one seamless experience (integrate customer data + channels + experience).

Five customer network strategies: Access (faster, easier, everywhere, always on — Tesco QR virtual stores), Engage (valued content, think like a media company — Blendtec), Customize (Netflix recommendations), Connect (be part of conversations, social listening — LEGO), Collaborate (customers help build — Waze, CNN iReport, crowdfunding).
Personalization = company adapts automatically using data. Customization = customer actively chooses.
CRM collects customer info, purchase history, preferences, interactions. Social CRM extends to social networks. Social listening monitors online conversations.
Customer network strategy generator: objectives → customers → strategy → concept → impact.

Mass customization (Gilmore & Pine): collaborative (product & representation change, e.g. Nike), adaptive (standard product users alter themselves), cosmetic (standard product presented differently, e.g. Nutella names), transparent (customized without customer knowing, e.g. Amazon/Netflix).
Product-centric vs customer-centric competition: focus on meeting individual needs across divisions and over time.
cards: Four traits of the new consumer
Multichannel: several channels. Omnichannel: channels integrated into one seamless experience.
Personalization: company adapts for you using data. Customization: you actively choose.
Engage = create valued content; Connect = participate in conversations; Collaborate = customers help create value.
Monitoring online conversations about the company, products, competitors and topics to spot opinions, problems, trends, opportunities.
Gilmore & Pine: four types of mass customization
Unique offering without customers explicitly knowing it was customized (based on past behaviour, e.g. Amazon, Netflix).
Standard product presented differently to different users (e.g. Nutella jar with your name).

mcq.q: A retailer has a website, an app and stores, but stock, customer data and returns are not shared between them. This is:
mcq.e: Having many channels is not enough; omnichannel requires integration.

mcq.q: Blendtec's 'Will it blend?' product demonstration videos illustrate which customer network strategy?
mcq.e: Engage = become a source of valued content, think like a media company.

mcq.q: Waze users reporting traffic and accidents illustrates:
mcq.e: Customers actively help create value.

mcq.q: Netflix automatically recommending shows based on viewing history is:
o: Cosmetic customization chosen by the user
mcq.e: The company adapts automatically using data.

mcq.q: Tesco's QR-code virtual stores in subway stations illustrate:
mcq.e: Access = faster, easier, everywhere, always on.

mcq.q: Which is the correct sequence of the customer network strategy generator?
mcq.e: Set the objective and target customer first, then choose strategy and develop a concrete concept, then define impact.

mcq.q: Which trait of the new consumer is described as 'communicating with each other and influencing companies through reviews and communities'?
mcq.e: Networked consumers influence companies via UGC, reviews, social media.

mcq.q: In Gilmore & Pine's framework, a company that changes the product for each customer through dialogue (e.g. Nike by You) uses:
mcq.e: Collaborative: dialogue to articulate needs and build a customized product.

tf: Customization means the customer actively chooses how the product is adapted.
Personalization is the company adapting automatically.
The digital customer journey is strictly linear.
It is non-linear: customers loop back, compare, switch.

topics.title: New buyer profile (B2B) & demand generation
summary: B2B operates in an extended enterprise: stand-alone competition → network rivalry.
Three peculiarities of B2B: relational nature, interdependencies, evolutionary dynamics.
B2B interaction model: environment, atmosphere (power/dependence, cooperation), interaction process (short-term exchanges), long-term relationships (institutionalization, adaptation).
Rolls-Royce Trent XWB: additive manufacturing co-created with Arcam AB, Sheffield University, Manufacturing Technology Centre.
B2B buyer: organizations, professional roles, documented criteria, long processes, high value, few customers, long-term relationships.
DMU/buying centre roles: initiator, user, influencer, decision-maker, buyer, gatekeeper. The user is not necessarily the one who authorizes or buys.
B2B purchasing process (6 stages): need recognition → specification → supplier search → evaluation & selection → contract & order routine → performance feedback.
Marketing funnel: awareness → consideration → action/decision → loyalty → advocacy.
Demand generation: lead generation → lead management → sales conversion → post-purchase.
Lead generation = buyer personas (semi-fictional ideal customer) + prospect collection (internal, external, active external, online external).
SEO = organic (non-paid); SEA = paid search ads; GEO = visibility in AI-generated answers. Qualified traffic = actively searching.
Prospect → qualified lead when closeness (fits ideal profile) + interest (downloads, requests, CTA).
Lead management = nurturing (right content, right moment, right customer — e.g. ABB) + scoring (profile + behaviour) + LMS.
Lead scoring example: 3 profile + 3 behaviour criteria, −5..+5 each, threshold +10 on both. High activity alone ≠ qualified.
Sales conversion: involve relevant DMU members, clarify, memo, close or recycle into nurturing. Post-purchase → loyalty & advocacy.
cards: Initiator, user, influencer, decision-maker, buyer, gatekeeper
Controls the flow of information to the buying group
Need recognition → specification → supplier search → evaluation & selection → contract & order routine → performance feedback
Lead generation → lead management → sales conversion → post-purchase
SEO: organic ranking. SEA: paid search ads. GEO: being cited/recommended in AI-generated answers.
When does a prospect become a qualified lead?
Closeness (fits ideal customer profile) + interest (demonstrated through actions).
Semi-fictional representation of an ideal customer based on research and real data (role, industry, goals, criteria, channels).
Internal, external (bought lists), active external (fairs, meetings), online external (webinars, website, publications)
Right content + right moment + right customer

mcq.q: In a buying centre, the person who controls the flow of information to the group is the:
mcq.e: Gatekeeper controls information flow; influencer provides technical info; initiator identifies the need.

mcq.q: Which activity is SEA?
o: Paying for ads that appear in search engine results
Improving meta descriptions to rank organically
Optimizing content so ChatGPT recommends the brand
mcq.e: SEA = paid search advertising.

mcq.q: A lead has profile score +12 and behaviour score +15, with a +10 threshold on each. The lead is:
o: Not sales-ready because profile is too low
Not sales-ready because behaviour is too high
mcq.e: Both dimensions ≥ +10 → sales-ready (Contact 1 in the lecture example).

mcq.q: A contact downloads every e-book and attends every webinar, but works in an industry and company size you never serve. What is the correct conclusion?
o: Not qualified: high activity alone does not make someone a qualified buyer
Qualified, because behaviour is what matters
Should be passed immediately to sales
Should be removed from all lists permanently
mcq.e: A lead must also fit the ideal customer profile (closeness).

mcq.q: Which is the correct order of demand generation?
o: Lead generation → lead management → sales conversion → post-purchase
Lead management → lead generation → post-purchase → sales conversion
Sales conversion → lead generation → lead management → post-purchase
Lead generation → sales conversion → lead management → post-purchase
mcq.e: Attract → nurture/score → convert → retain.

mcq.q: GEO stands for and means:
o: Generative Engine Optimization: being mentioned/cited by AI-powered search and chatbots
Geographic Expansion Operations: entering new regions
Google Enterprise Optimization: paid Google campaigns
mcq.e: GEO = visibility in AI-generated answers.

mcq.q: If a sales conversion fails, what does the lecture recommend?
o: Recycle the lead into lead nurturing
mcq.e: Unsuccessful leads may be recycled into nurturing rather than discarded.

mcq.q: Which statement about internal vs external prospect lists is correct?
o: Internal lists are lower cost and more qualified but limited and slow to build
External lists are cheaper and always more qualified
Internal lists are immediately available in large numbers
External lists require no purchasing cost
mcq.e: External lists: immediate, large, but costly and possibly unqualified.

mcq.q: The Rolls-Royce Trent XWB case mainly demonstrates that:
o: Innovation and value can be co-created through a network of specialized partners
SEO is more important than trade fairs
mcq.e: Arcam AB, Sheffield University and MTC co-created additive manufacturing capability.

mcq.q: Compared with B2C, B2B purchasing typically has:
o: Longer sales cycles, multiple participants and higher risk
More emotional promotion and lower investment

Divergent = explore: informal, open questions, qualitative, selected (not representative) customers, rough prototypes, early stage. Method: preparation → iteration → action.

topics.title: Innovation under constraints: open/closed, lean, agile
summary: Closed innovation: generate, develop and commercialize own ideas internally (Ford, GE, DuPont, Bell Labs). Pros: IP control, first mover, talent retention. Cons: high R&D cost, few external ideas, missed markets.
Open innovation (Henry Chesbrough, 2003): use internal and external ideas; permeable boundaries.
Drivers of open innovation: worker mobility, venture capital, rising R&D costs, shorter tech life cycles, market complexity, customer expectations, networks.

Requirements: open communication, collaboration, commitment, idea-sharing support, ability to integrate external knowledge, top-management support. Absorptive capacity = ability to recognize, absorb and use external knowledge.

Inbound (outside → in: LEGO Ideas, crowdsourcing, hackathons, universities); outbound (inside → out: licensing, spin-offs — Tesla 2014 patents; riskier); coupled (both: alliances, JVs — Oxford/AstraZeneca 2020).
Choice factors: complex innovation, objectives (specific short-term → closed; broad long-term → open), high competition (→ closed protects R&D). Open is not automatically superior.

topics.title: Disruptive business models
summary: Business disruption: a challenger offers significantly greater customer value in a way incumbents cannot directly compete with. Digital enables connect, scale, recombine.

Schumpeter (1942) creative destruction: innovation replaces old structures (carriages → cars; ice → refrigeration; candles → electric light).
Christensen's innovator's dilemma: good management (listening to best customers) can cause failure; disruptors look unattractive (inferior, low margins, small market).

Christensen's disruption: incumbents overshoot; entrants start cheaper/simpler at the low end or with non-consumers, improve, move upmarket, displace. Takes years (Wikipedia 2001 → Britannica print ends 2012).
Low-end disruption targets the least profitable existing customers; new-market disruption targets non-consumers.
Digital disruption trajectory: faint signals → validated model → critical mass → scale & maturity. Respond before critical mass.
Innovation types: incremental, sustaining (better for existing customers), radical (technological breakthrough), disruptive (changes competitive structure). Radical ≠ disruptive.

Limitations of Christensen: B2B origin; doesn't explain disruption driven by consumers, starting with core customers, or benefits beyond price (iPhone vs Nokia).

topics.title: Modularity, service modularity & servitization
summary: Faster innovation (digitalization, sustainability) + price pressure (commoditization, globalization) → three approaches: modularity, service modularity, servitization.
Standardization: high cost efficiency, low variety. Customization: low efficiency, high variety. Modularity: high + high.
Modularity = independently designed modules functioning as an integrated whole; fewer unique building blocks for more configurations (LEGO). An organizational mindset.
Product architecture: functions, modules, interfaces, standards (compatibility & performance comparison).
Performance: efficiency (fewer building blocks), flexibility (more products from existing modules), agility (fewer new components to expand).

assignments.title: Disruptive Business Model Map: Galeries Lafayette vs YOOX Net-a-Porter
assignments.badge: Based on a past exam case
assignments.prompt: Using Rogers' Disruptive Business Model Map, assess whether YOOX Net-a-Porter (challenger) represents a disruptive threat to Galeries Lafayette (incumbent). Compare target customers, value propositions and value networks, apply the two-part test, and discuss customer trajectory, disruptive scope and possible incumbent responses.
model: Frame

Challenger: YOOX Net-a-Porter (digital luxury retailer). Incumbent: Galeries Lafayette (physical luxury department store). Rogers: disruption = clash of asymmetric business models; requires both a VP differential and a VN differential.
Customers

GL: customers valuing physical shopping, human contact, tourists, loyal luxury shoppers. YNAP: digital-first luxury buyers, younger customers, international customers without store access. Partial overlap.
Value proposition

GL: human contact, aggregation of brands under one roof, physical shopping experience, customer loyalty. YNAP: easy access anytime/anywhere, wider choice, exclusivity (capsule collections), appeal to younger customers. VP differentials (Rogers' nine): access, aggregation, personalization.
Value network

GL: prestigious location, reputation, collaboration with important brands, physical stores. YNAP: e-commerce infrastructure, data assets, recommendation engines, capsule collections with brands, logistics. VN differentials: channels, data assets, cost structure, skills & processes.
Two-part test

1) Radical displacement of value? Partially — YNAP replaces many purchase occasions but not the experiential, human side of the store. 2) Barrier to imitation? Yes for GL: building data assets, recommendation engines, global logistics and a digital culture is costly and could cannibalize stores.
Three variables

Customer trajectory: largely inside-out (mainstream luxury buyers online) plus outside-in (younger/remote non-consumers). Disruptive scope: partial (specific use cases and segments). Other incumbents: luxury brands' own boutiques, other department stores, multi-brand boutiques.
Verdict & responses

A significant but partial disruptive threat. GL could become the disruptor (launch its own platform, acquire a digital player, split a separate digital unit) or mitigate losses (refocus on experiential flagship stores and tourists, diversify into events/services). Recommended: launch/omnichannel + refocus on experience.

model: Christensen

Disruption starts outside the mainstream: low-end (least profitable existing customers) or new-market (non-consumers) with simpler, cheaper, initially inferior products; incumbents overshoot; entrants improve and move upmarket. Focus: WHERE disruption begins; mechanism = performance trajectory. Limitations: B2B origin, misses consumer-driven disruption, inside-out trajectories, non-price benefits (iPhone).
Rogers

Disruption = clash of asymmetric business models. Requires a VP differential (radically different customer value) + VN differential (barrier to imitation). Trajectory can be outside-in or inside-out; benefits beyond price. Focus: WHY incumbents cannot copy. Adds customer trajectory, disruptive scope, other incumbents.
Uber — Christensen
Not disruptive: entered the mainstream market first (existing taxi users) with a better experience → sustaining innovation (lecture classification).
Uber — Rogers

Arguably disruptive: VP differentials (access via app, simplicity, cashless payment, price transparency, ratings); VN differentials (no owned vehicles, driver network, dynamic pricing, data, network effects) that taxi firms cannot easily replicate. Trajectory inside-out.
Netflix — Christensen
Disruptive: started with a niche, accessible, initially lower-performing alternative (DVD by mail) and improved, eventually displacing Blockbuster.
Netflix — Rogers

Disruptive: VP (no late fees, home delivery, wider selection, recommendations) + VN (subscription model, e-commerce site, warehouses/mail distribution, data/recommendation engine, no retail costs). Disruption began before streaming.
Conclusion
Theories agree on Netflix but diverge on Uber: Christensen is narrower (entry point), Rogers broader (business model asymmetry). Rogers better explains digital-economy disruption.
checklist: Defined Christensen's low-end and new-market disruption
Defined Rogers' two conditions (VP + VN differential)
Contrasted focus: where it starts vs why incumbents can't copy
Uber classified as sustaining under Christensen with reason
Uber analysed with Rogers' VP and VN

assignments.title: Value Proposition Canvas and Ad-Lib for a food delivery app
assignments.prompt: A food delivery start-up targets busy university students. Build a Value Proposition Canvas (customer profile and value map), assess the fit, identify the functional, emotional and social jobs (JTBD), and write a value proposition using the Ad-Lib template. Suggest a USP and check it against the five USP characteristics.
model: Approach
Start from the customer (empathy canvas: what they see, say, do, hear, think & feel), then design the value map. Fit = value map addresses the most important and intense jobs, pains and gains.
Customer jobs
Functional: eat a decent meal quickly between lectures/study. Emotional: feel in control, less stressed, cared for. Social: eat with friends, not look broke, share food.
Pains
Limited budget, delivery fees, long waiting, unhealthy options, minimum order values, uncertainty about delivery time.
Gains
Low price, speed, healthy choices, group ordering, student discounts, predictable timing, loyalty rewards.
Value map

Products & services: app with student-priced menus, campus pickup lockers, group orders. Pain relievers: no fee on campus lockers, split-bill, live tracking, low minimum order. Gain creators: student subscription, healthy meal bundles, loyalty points, study-time scheduled delivery.
Ad-Lib

Our campus food app helps busy university students who want to eat well between lectures by eliminating delivery fees and waiting uncertainty and creating affordable healthy group meals, unlike general delivery apps with high fees and minimum orders.
USP

'Free delivery to campus lockers in 15 minutes.' Easy to understand ✓, verifiable ✓, unique (if competitors lack lockers) ✓, not temporary (requires locker network — VN barrier) ✓, value-driven (relieves top pains) ✓. Position in the 'winning zone'.
checklist: Identified functional, emotional AND social jobs
Built value map: products/services, pain relievers, gain creators mapped to pains/gains
Proposed a USP and checked the five characteristics

assignments.title: Value Proposition Roadmap for a traditional bookstore chain
assignments.prompt: A national chain of physical bookstores is losing customers to Amazon, e-books and audiobook subscriptions. Apply Rogers' six-step Value Proposition Roadmap and classify value elements as core, weakened, disrupted and new, with the strategic action for each. Conclude with a forward-looking value proposition.
model: 1. Customer types
Avid readers, students, gift buyers, families with children, tourists, local community/schools.
2. Current value
Browsing and discovery, expert staff advice, immediate availability, gift wrapping, events and author signings, a pleasant place to spend time.
3. Emerging threats
Amazon (price, selection, delivery), e-books/Kindle, audiobook subscriptions, TikTok/BookTok discovery, social platforms for reviews.
4. Assess elements

Core: curated discovery, expert advice, community/events, physical experience. Weakened: availability/selection (Amazon wider), price. Disrupted: pure transactional purchase of known titles. New: still to be created.
5. New elements

Book subscription boxes curated by staff, BookTok-inspired tables, café/co-working, kids' reading programmes, membership with events, click-and-collect from online catalogue, local author marketplace.
Actions

Core → build on (events, curation). Weakened → bolster (omnichannel: online catalogue + 24h pickup, price-match on bestsellers for members). Disrupted → deprioritize (stop competing on long-tail inventory). New → create (memberships, community spaces, subscriptions).
6. Forward-looking VP
'The place where readers discover their next favourite book and meet others who love it — in store, online and in your mailbox.'
checklist: All six roadmap steps in order
Correct actions: build on / bolster / deprioritize / create

assignments.title: Data Value Generator for a gym chain
assignments.prompt: A mid-sized gym chain wants to reduce member churn. Apply the Data Value Generator (all five steps). Specify KPIs, choose and justify value templates, describe a concept, perform a data audit (available data, gaps, sources), and propose an execution plan. Mention challenges and the three myths of big data.
model: 1. Impact & KPIs
Objective: reduce churn and increase engagement. KPIs: monthly churn rate, visits per member per month, renewal rate, class booking rate, NPS.
2. Value templates

Insight: discover patterns preceding cancellation (falling visit frequency). Targeting: identify at-risk members (micro-segments, CLV). Personalization: tailored workout plans and offers. Context: show members progress vs their own history and benchmarks (quantified self).
3. Concept
Early-warning churn model + app that personalizes plans and nudges at-risk members (trainer call, free class), with progress dashboards.
4. Data audit

Available: check-ins, membership contracts, class bookings, payments. Gaps: workout data, satisfaction feedback, wearable data, reasons for cancellation. Sources: customer value data exchange (app features in exchange for wearable data), lead users (super-users testing features), public data (weather, holidays), partners (wearable brands).
5. Execution

Technical: integrate CRM, app and access systems (combine silos), cloud analytics. Processes: trainers act on alerts. Pilot in 2 gyms vs 2 control gyms (convergent experiment), measure churn, then scale.
Challenges & myths

Data skills, data quality, silos, privacy/GDPR & customer trust (transparent value exchange). Myths: algorithm won't do everything (trainers needed), correlation ≠ causation (low visits may follow injury), small structured data (check-ins) is already valuable.
checklist: Concrete concept explaining how data improves the KPI
Data audit with available data, gaps and named sources
Execution plan with pilot/proof of concept
Referenced the myths of big data

assignments.title: Platform strategy for a tutoring marketplace
assignments.prompt: You are launching a platform connecting university students with peer tutors. Using the platform frameworks from the course, analyse: participants and value exchanged, platform type, network effects (direct and cross-side), how to solve the chicken-and-egg problem, governance and trust, revenue models, and competitors (symmetric and asymmetric). Would this create disintermediation or intermediation?
model: Participants & value
Students (get affordable help, flexibility) ↔ tutors (earn money, CV experience); possibly universities and advertisers. Platform provides matching, scheduling, payments, ratings.
Platform type & properties
Exchange platform (service marketplace). Distinct groups ✓, direct interaction (tutors set profiles/prices) ✓, facilitation ✓.
Network effects
Cross-side: more tutors → more subjects/availability → more students → more demand → more tutors. Direct: more students → more study groups/content shared. Data loop: more sessions → better matching.
Critical mass

Start with one university and high-demand courses; seed tutors with fee waivers; use student associations; free trial sessions. Scaling via frictionless acquisition (app, university login), trust and mobile access.
Governance & trust
Who can be a tutor (grade verification), ratings and reviews, refund policy, payment escrow, rules against academic misconduct, ranking algorithm, fee rules, data ownership.
Revenue
Transaction fee per session, membership (student premium), services (exam bootcamps), advertising (limited). Combine models.
Competitors
Symmetric: other tutoring marketplaces. Asymmetric: AI tutors/ChatGPT, YouTube, university tutoring services, study groups. Co-opetition possible with universities.
Intermediation
Mostly intermediation: platform inserts itself between tutors and students who used to meet informally, capturing value — but also disintermediates traditional tutoring agencies.
checklist: Classified platform type with the three properties
Explained direct AND cross-side network effects
Governance questions (access, ranking, fees, data, trust)

assignments.title: Customer Network Strategy Generator for a cosmetics brand
assignments.prompt: A mid-market cosmetics brand sells mainly through supermarkets and is losing young customers to digitally native brands. Describe the new consumer profile, then use the Customer Network Strategy Generator (objectives → customers → strategy → concept → impact) to design an initiative using at least two of the five customer network strategies. Explain how to make the experience omnichannel.
model: New consumer
Hyper-informed (reviews, ingredient apps), less loyal (easy switching), omnichannel (TikTok → store → online), networked (influencers, UGC). Non-linear journey.
Objective
Increase share among 18–28-year-olds and repeat purchases.
Customers
Gen Z skincare enthusiasts active on TikTok/Instagram; secondary: price-conscious students.
Strategies

Engage: tutorial content and ingredient education (think like a media company). Collaborate: co-create a product line with community voting (crowdsourcing). Customize/personalize: AI skin-analysis in the app recommending routines. Connect: social listening and community responses.
Concept
'Create With Us' app + community: users vote on new shades, submit routines, get personalized recommendations; winning product sold in store with the co-creators' names (cosmetic customization).
Impact
KPIs: app downloads, UGC volume, community engagement, repeat purchase rate, share of 18–28 buyers; level of customer involvement.
Omnichannel
Integrate customer data, channels and experience: QR codes on shelves → tutorials; online basket redeemable in store; loyalty points across channels; CRM/social CRM unifying profiles.
checklist: Described the four traits of the new consumer
Used at least two customer network strategies correctly
Distinguished personalization vs customization where relevant

assignments.title: Demand generation plan for an industrial robot supplier
assignments.prompt: An Italian SME sells collaborative robots to manufacturers. Describe the DMU at a typical customer, then design a demand generation plan across the four stages: lead generation (buyer persona, prospect sources, SEO/SEA/GEO), lead management (nurturing and a lead scoring model with thresholds), sales conversion and post-purchase.
model: DMU

Initiator: production manager noticing bottlenecks. User: line operators. Influencer: process engineers, safety officer, external consultant. Decision-maker: plant manager/CFO. Buyer: purchasing department. Gatekeeper: assistant or IT/procurement controlling supplier info.
Buyer persona

'Marco, plant manager, 45, mid-size food packaging firm (50–250 employees), goals: productivity and worker safety, constraints: budget, integration with existing lines, prefers case studies and trade fairs, reads industry publications.'
Prospect sources

Internal (existing customers' contacts, CRM), external (purchased databases of manufacturers), active external (trade fairs like automation fairs, plant visits), online external (webinars, website, publications).
SEO / SEA / GEO
SEO: content on 'cobot for packaging' keywords. SEA: paid ads on high-intent searches. GEO: authoritative case studies and specs so AI assistants cite the brand.
Lead management

Nurturing: right content at the right moment — ROI calculator, case studies, webinars, demo videos. Scoring: profile (industry, size, role/authority, project timeframe) and behaviour (pricing page visit, webinar, ROI calculator use) each −5..+5, threshold e.g. +10 on both before sales handoff. LMS/CRM tracks prospect → cold → hot → sales-ready.
Sales conversion
Meetings with decision-makers, influencers and buyers; clarify requirements; on-site demo; memo confirmed by customer; close or recycle into nurturing.
Post-purchase
Installation, training, maintenance contracts (servitization), performance reviews → loyalty and advocacy (referenceable case studies).
checklist: All six DMU roles applied to the case
Lead scoring with profile + behaviour and threshold

assignments.title: Experimentation plan and launch strategy for a new app feature
assignments.prompt: A bike-sharing company wants to introduce a 'group ride' feature. Design (a) a divergent experiment and (b) a convergent experiment (with hypothesis, variables, groups and metric). Then use the two launch criteria to choose a launch strategy and connect your plan to at least four of the seven principles of start-up thinking.
model: Divergent

Explore: give a rough prototype (clickable mock-up) to selected users (students, tourists, cycling clubs); open-ended interviews and observation; qualitative feedback; generate several solutions; persevere or pivot. Method: preparation → iteration → action.
Convergent

Hypothesis: offering a 15% group discount increases rides per user. Independent variable: group-ride feature with discount shown. Dependent variable: rides per active user per week. Control: current app; treatment: new feature. Random assignment of a representative sample; statistically valid; analyse, decide, share learning.
Launch criteria
Can iterate quickly? Yes (app updates). Can limit rollout? Yes (by city or user group). → MVP roll-out: basic version in one city, improve with feedback, then expand.
Principles

Learn early (prototype before building), be fast & iterate, fall in love with the problem (people want to ride together safely and cheaply), get credible feedback (right samples), measure what matters now (rides, not app opens), test assumptions, fail smart (cheap, early, shared).
checklist: Divergent experiment: selected sample, qualitative, rough prototype
Convergent experiment: hypothesis, independent & dependent variables

assignments.title: Open vs closed innovation and Lean for a furniture manufacturer
assignments.prompt: A traditional furniture manufacturer with a large internal R&D department wants to innovate faster and cut costs. Recommend whether and how it should adopt open innovation (which type: inbound, outbound or coupled), explain the role of absorptive capacity and false negatives, and propose how Lean principles and the DOWNTIME wastes, together with Agile methods, could improve operations.
model: Closed today
Internal R&D, IP control, but high cost and limited external ideas; risk of missing opportunities.
Recommendation

Adopt open innovation selectively. Factors: complexity (smart furniture needs electronics expertise → open), objectives (long-term new categories → open; specific short-term upgrades → closed), competition (protect core designs).
Types

Inbound: design competitions, crowdsourcing (like LEGO Ideas), collaboration with design schools and start-ups. Outbound: license unused patents (e.g. joint mechanisms), spin-offs. Coupled: joint venture with an electronics firm for smart desks.
Absorptive capacity & false negatives

Needs the ability to recognize and integrate external knowledge (scouts, open culture, top-management support). Rejected internal ideas can be licensed or spun off — rescuing false negatives (Xerox PARC lesson).
Lean

Five principles: identify value → map value stream → flow → pull (produce to order) → perfection. Attack DOWNTIME: defects (quality checks/jidoka), overproduction and inventory (JIT, pull), waiting, non-utilized talent (kaizen suggestions), transportation and motion (layout), extra-processing.
Agile
Cross-functional teams iterate new product designs (design → build → test → learn). Lean = efficiency; Agile = adaptability — complementary.

assignments.title: Modularity and servitization for a coffee machine producer
assignments.prompt: A producer of professional coffee machines for cafés faces price competition from Asian manufacturers. Explain how modularity (architecture, performance dimensions, three stages) and servitization (four levels, objectives, implications) could help. Distinguish co-creation from co-production and discuss sustainability.
model: Modularity

Design platform architecture: functions (brew, grind, steam), modules (boiler, grinder, interface), interfaces and standards. Efficiency: fewer building blocks; flexibility: many configurations (1–4 groups, milk modules); agility: few new parts for new models. Stages: modular-in-production (economies of scale on modules), modular-in-design (upgrade grinder independently), modular-in-use (cafés configure machines).
Servitization levels

1 tangible machine → 2 + supporting services (installation, repairs) → 3 + differentiating services (remote IoT monitoring, predictive maintenance, barista training) → 4 product as a service (pay per cup / monthly subscription including maintenance).
Objectives
Recurring revenue, loyalty, longer relationships, differentiation beyond price.
Implications
Changes in strategy, processes, skills (service technicians, data), investments (IoT, financing), culture, relational capabilities.
Co-creation vs co-production
Co-creation: value emerges in use, e.g. data from café usage improves recipes. Co-production: cafés co-design a custom machine line and share investment.
Sustainability
Modules can be repaired, upgraded, refurbished; PaaS facilitates take-back and remanufacturing → circular economy.

assignments.title: Designing an AI agent for customer service, with governance
assignments.prompt: An insurance company wants to deploy an AI agent that handles claims from first contact to payout proposal. Explain how it differs from a chatbot and a copilot, describe its four components and its loop, identify the five risks and how to mitigate them, propose governance under the four requirements, and discuss how AI could reshape the company's operating and business model.
model: Chatbot → copilot → agent
Chatbot answers policy questions; copilot drafts claim assessments for a human; agent plans and executes the claim process with tools toward a goal.
Components

LLM core (reasoning), planner (break claim into steps: collect info, verify policy, assess damage photos, estimate, propose payout), tools (CRM, policy database, image-damage estimation, payment system via APIs/MCP), memory (short-term: claim context; long-term: customer history).
Loop
Perceive (claim, photos) → reason (next step) → act (query policy DB, request documents) → observe results → repeat.
Risks & mitigation

Amplified hallucinations → verification steps, confidence thresholds; cost & latency → limit steps; prompt injection via uploaded documents → input sanitization, restricted tools; uncontrolled autonomy → human approval above a payout threshold; hard ROI → define KPIs (handling time, cost per claim, satisfaction) and pilot.
Governance

Written policies (what the agent may approve), traceability (logs of each decision), human oversight (stop/override), governance ownership (named claims manager). EU AI Act risk-based approach; insurance decisions may be high-risk.
Ethics
Bias in training data (debiasing), transparency to customers, accountability.
Operating & business model

AI-driven operating model (automated claims, fraud detection) can reshape the business model: instant payouts as a VP differential, usage-based policies, new services. Humans remain central for ambiguity, empathy, value judgments.

assignments.title: From Industry 3.0 to 4.0 (and 5.0) in a car-parts factory
assignments.prompt: A car-parts factory uses computerized machines and robots that operate separately. Explain why it is Industry 3.0, describe what would make it Industry 4.0 (technologies, smart factory, predictive maintenance, push vs pull), how Physical AI and cobots could be introduced, and what Industry 5.0 principles would add. Discuss implications for workers.
model: Diagnosis
Automation (programmed tasks) without interconnection/data exchange = Industry 3.0. An automated machine is not automatically 4.0.
To 4.0

IoT sensors on machines (temperature, vibration), CPS adjusting parameters automatically, cloud and big data analytics, AI optimization, digital twin of the line to simulate changes. Smart factory benefits: real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance (fix before breakdown), flexible production, less downtime.
Push → pull
Move from forecast-driven batches to demand-triggered production linked to carmakers' orders (JIT), reducing overproduction risk while managing delay risk.
Physical AI & cobots
Perceive–decide–act robots; cobots for ergonomically hard tasks (like PART4you); move toward selective dark-factory cells. Data loop improves models.
Industry 5.0
Human-centricity (technology supports workers), sustainability (energy efficiency, less waste), resilience (adapt to supply shocks).
Workers

Role shifts from programming/supervising to working with connected systems and collaborating; tasks eliminated, transformed, created (predictive maintenance specialist, AI–robot integration expert). Reskilling vs upskilling; skills gap is the main challenge. VUCA context requires adaptability.
checklist: Named 4.0 technologies (IoT, CPS, AI, cloud, digital twin)

assignments.title: Analysing Green Srl's business model transformation
assignments.prompt: Using course frameworks, analyse how Green Srl transformed the traditional energy business model. Discuss the problems of the traditional market, the value proposition shift, the prosumer, ecosystem/platform logic, customer segments, and whether Green could be considered a disruptive challenger to traditional utilities (Rogers' two-part test).
model: Traditional market problems
Fragmentation (silos), commodity trap (kWh sold, price risk on customers), intermediation and speculation.
VP shift
From selling kWh to energy autonomy and long-term cost stabilization; risk reduction and independence (value categories: risk reduction, save money).
Prosumer
Customer as producer + consumer — collaborate strategy; customer participates in value creation.
Ecosystem logic
SeLea integrates production, technology, users, finance, grids and market operators — orchestration of participants; Independent, Open (open innovation), Advanced; component-oriented (modularity).
Segments (multi-sided VP)
Home: savings through self-production. Business: cost protection. Welfare: employees' purchasing power. SeLinvest: investors in real assets.
Disruption test

VP differential: autonomy/cost stability vs commodity kWh — significant for target segments. VN differential: integrated ecosystem, Italian renewable assets, financing model without incentives, multidisciplinary know-how → hard for utilities to replicate without cannibalizing. Scope partial; trajectory starting with families and SMEs. Double Jump Theory = anticipating the market.
checklist: Three problems of the traditional market
Rogers' two-part test applied with verdict
